analysis.one_liner: Extends overtime pay protections to agricultural workers, phasing down to 40 hours a week.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 11 cosponsors (all Democrats or independents), never left the Senate committee it was assigned to, and no vote was ever taken before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to require farm employers to pay time-and-a-half for long workweeks, starting at 55 hours in 2023 and stepping down to 40 hours by 2026 (smaller farms get a later start). It would also repeal the decades-old exemption that has allowed agricultural employers — including small farms, irrigation projects, sugar processors, and cotton gins — to skip overtime pay entirely. Like most bills, it never got that far: it was assigned to a committee and never came back out.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly two million people who work in America's fields, orchards, and packing sheds would gain the same overtime right most other workers have had since the 1930s. Farm work is seasonal and hours run long at harvest time, so time-and-a-half after 40–55 hours would mean real money for workers who today are paid straight time no matter how long they work. The bill also removes exemptions for related industries such as sugar processing and cotton ginning, extending the pay right to more food-sector workers [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Farm workers paid straight time for long weeks

how_it_helps.text: Requires agricultural employers to pay 1.5 times the regular rate for hours over 55 in 2023, 50 in 2024, 45 in 2025, and 40 from 2026 onward, for employers with more than 25 employees.
Gives employers with 25 or fewer employees a delayed phase-in: overtime starts in 2026 at 55 hours and reaches the 40-hour standard in 2029.

Repeals the overtime exemptions for agriculture-related employers, including certain small farms, irrigation projects, sugar processing, and cotton ginning and compressing, while preserving the carve-out for members of the employer's immediate family.
Closes off a separate small-farm overtime exemption in the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act by tying its definition to the updated Fair Labor Standards Act rules.

analysis.who_pays: Agricultural employers would bear the cost of the additional wages, with labor-intensive growers affected most; some of that cost could reach consumers through food prices or lead growers to cut hours or substitute machinery. Farms with 25 or fewer employees get several extra years before the requirement applies [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Farm employers, and possibly food prices

drawbacks.text: Payroll costs would rise for growers, especially in labor-intensive crops; an honest supporter would acknowledge that some of the cost could show up in food prices, or lead growers to cap hours or speed mechanization.

The long phase-in limits the immediate benefit: employers with more than 25 employees keep the old rules until the new 55-hour threshold starts in 2023 and the repealed exemptions don't fully take effect until 2026, and small farms wait until 2026–2029, so the strongest protections arrive years after passage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to a low-paid, historically excluded workforce is direct and easy to see: overtime after a long week is exactly the protection the 1938 law gave almost everyone else while carving out farm workers. The costs are real but bounded — higher payroll costs for growers, likely spread partly into food prices, and softened by a multi-year phase-in and a small-farm delay. On balance the bill is a straightforward wage-protection measure whose main design concession (the slow timeline) also dilutes its early impact.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate committee that handles labor law, which never acted on it, and the two-year Congress ended without a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Alex Padilla introduced the bill on June 23, 2022, joined by 11 cosponsors — 10 Senate Democrats and 1 independent — and it was read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
No further action appears in the record: the committee never reported the bill, the Senate never debated it, and there was no roll-call vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
Because a new Congress began the next day, the bill died and would have to be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Agricultural employers are better off: because the bill never advanced, the overtime exemption for farm labor — and for related industries like sugar processing and cotton ginning — remains in place, and growers continue paying straight time for long weeks.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Farm employers, who keep paying no overtime

for.name: Sen. Alex Padilla
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fairness for Farm Workers Act and made introductory remarks.

for.name: 10 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate independents
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including Sens. Feinstein, Warren, Blumenthal, Booker, Sanders, Cortez Masto, Wyden, Van Hollen, Klobuchar, Brown, and Markey.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Patty Murray (D)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred; the record shows no markup, no report, and no vote.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor at any point in the roughly six months before the Congress ended.

against.name: 50 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No member cosponsored the bill, leaving it with no Republican support in a chamber where moving most legislation needs 60 votes.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan split was never measured; what the record shows is one-sided sponsorship — 11 Democrats and independents, zero Republicans — and a Senate whose majority party did not move the bill itself.

industries.industry: Fruit, vegetable, and other labor-intensive farming
industries.note: These growers employ most of the country's field and harvest workers and would owe time-and-a-half after long weeks, cutting into a business model that has relied on paying straight time for extended hours. The multi-year phase-in and small-farm delay soften but do not remove the cost.

industries.industry: Agriculture-related processing (sugar processing, cotton ginning and compressing, irrigation projects)
industries.note: The bill repeals their specific overtime exemptions from the Fair Labor Standards Act, subjecting them to the same overtime rules as other employers.
